hints: Because the input intervals are already sorted and non-overlapping, you do not need to sort them again.
First copy every interval whose end is strictly before newInterval's start.
Merge intervals while their start is less than or equal to the current end of the new interval.
After the merge finishes, append all remaining intervals unchanged.
title: Insert Interval Problem

notes: Intervals are closed, so intervals that touch at an endpoint are considered overlapping and must be merged.
constraints: intervals is sorted in ascending order by start_i and contains non-overlapping intervals
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: The new interval [2,5] overlaps [1,3], so they merge into [1,5], while [6,9] remains separate.
The new interval [4,8] overlaps [3,5], [6,7], and [8,10], so those intervals merge into [3,10].

content.problemStatement:
You receive an array of non-overlapping intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]` represent the start and the end of the `i^th` interval and `intervals` is sorted in ascending order by `start_i`. You are also given an interval `newInterval = [start, end]` that represents the start and end of another interval.

Insert `newInterval` into `intervals` such that `intervals` is still sorted in ascending order by `start_i` and `intervals` still does not have any overlapping intervals (merge overlapping intervals if necessary).

The task is to output `intervals` *after the insertion*.

**Note** that you don't need to modify `intervals` in-place. You can make a new array and output it.

notes: Solutions are judged against the JSON-serialised return value.
Because the input is already sorted and non-overlapping, no sorting is required.
Overlap uses intervals[i][0] <= currentEnd and non-overlap before insertion uses intervals[i][1] < currentStart.
solution.approach: Scan the intervals from left to right in three phases: copy intervals completely before the new interval, merge every interval that overlaps or touches the new interval, then append the remaining intervals.

better.complexity: O(log n + k) comparisons to locate and merge the affected region, plus O(n) to materialize the returned result in the worst case.
better.description: Use binary search to locate the first interval whose end can reach the new interval, then scan only the potentially affected suffix while preserving the already ordered prefix. The final result still requires O(n) output space and, in the worst case, O(n) total work.

optimal.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for the returned array.
optimal.description: Exploit the sorted, non-overlapping input directly. First copy intervals ending before the new interval starts. Then expand the new interval while existing intervals start at or before its current end. Finally append all untouched intervals. The invariant is that every copied prefix interval is strictly before the merged interval and every skipped interval overlaps or touches it.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the combined list/result.
bruteForce.description: Append newInterval to the existing intervals, sort all intervals by start, and then perform a standard merge pass. This is correct but performs unnecessary sorting because the original intervals are already sorted.

solution.timeComplexity: O(n), where n is the number of existing intervals.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the returned interval array.

followUps: Can the returned result be constructed while modifying the input array in place?
How would the approach change if the input intervals were not sorted?
What changes would be needed if intervals that only touch at an endpoint were not considered overlapping?
